text_1.eng: Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperatures and weather patterns.

rows.title: Climate Change Adaptation

text_1.eng: This is the process of adjusting farming methods to reduce the risks caused by shifting weather patterns.

rows.title: Climate Change

text_1.eng:
**These changes include:**
 * Strong dry winds 
 * Prolonged droughts 
 * Acid rains 
 * Unpredictable rains and floods
 * High humidity 
 * Increases in strange weeds (invasive species) 
 * Increase in sunlight intensity and temperature

rows.title: Minimizing water evaporation

text_1.eng: Farmers can reduce the amount of soil moisture that is lost through evaporation by:

section_1_text.eng: Planting trees or using shade nets keeps crops and soil cooler and moist, reduces water loss, protects plants from strong wind and weather, and improves soil while allowing other crops to grow.

section_2_text.eng: Mulching uses dry or live cover to reduce water loss, protect soil, improve fertility, and support soil organisms.

rows.title: Embracing Agrobiodiversity

text_1.eng: Diversifying crops and livestock ensures multiple harvests throughout the season and protects your food supply if drought causes one crop to fail.

section_1_text.eng: * Cultivating diverse, drought-tolerant fodder crops ensures year-round animal health and productivity while improving soil carbon storage.

section_1_extra_text.eng:
* Drought-tolerant grasses (e.g., Napier or Rhodes)
 * Legumes (e.g., Alfalfa or Cowpeas)
 * Fodder trees (e.g., Calliandra or Sesbania)
 * Stored silage/hay

rows.title: Managing excess water

section_1_text.eng:
* Raised beds lift the soil above ground level, so excess water drains away and roots do not rot.
 * The soil also warms up faster and keeps moisture better, helping crops in both wet and dry seasons.

section_1_text.eng:
* Plant crops along the slope lines (not straight up and down).
 * This slows water flow, stops soil erosion, and saves fertile topsoil.
 * Keeps good yields even when weather changes a lot.

section_1_text.eng: * These crops grow well in waterlogged or flooded areas. * They keep food production going when rains are too much. * Examples: rice, arrowroots, and bananas.

section_2_text.eng:
* Dig channels to remove extra water from heavy rains and floods.
 * This lowers the water table and reduces runoff on the farm.
 * Plant water-tolerant crops like bananas and arrowroots along the channels.

rows.title: Microcatchments:

text_1.eng: Ensure you watch videos in the 'Practical Section' on how to make Zai pits and Sunken beds and the tool used.

section_1_text.eng:
* These are small, individual basins (usually 20–30 cm deep) dug into the soil.
 * They are filled with a mixture of **manure** or **compost** to improve fertility and water-holding capacity.

section_2_text.eng:
* These are large rectangular or circular areas dug out so the planting surface is below the surrounding ground level.
 * The ***"sunken"*** design captures surface runoff and protects young seedlings from drying winds.
 * These beds maintain a cooler, more humid environment for leafy vegetables and herbs.
